questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to visit a country that was culturally different from Denmark. An important aspect in choosing the university was how much focus was put on their international program and the opportunities given to exchange students.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The overall experience was great and I would definitely recommend Yonsei to anyone who dreams of studying in Seoul. My only 'complaint' is how little information students were given about the academic expectations and their performance, which lead me to stressing unnecessarily over tests and thinking I would fail classes I ended up doing great in. So even though East Asian universities may seem academically daunting, and Yonsei being a part of SKY, one should not be discouraged from studying abroad.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Yonsei did a fine job of informing international students of the necessary deadlines etc. via email. We were always informed in due time, though that was sometimes only a few days in advance - I would have liked to receive the information a bit earlier (but that might just be my personal need to plan far in advance).

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The international help disk in the Global Lounge was of great help IF you personally reached out to them. With that said, my biggest complaint about being an international student at Yonsei was how many things we were left to deal with on our own or was poorly managed by the school. For one, the school did not inform us properly about exemption from NHIS (which you for sure will be able to get!), which I had to find out about through other exchange students. It wasn't a difficult process but it was quite difficult to find the correct documents and information about how to apply. In addition, my best advice would be to apply for the ARC on you own and NOT through the school (since this took aaaages and was really inconvenient) by either arriving in Seoul before the semester starts or booking an appointment at the immigration office near Yonsei BEFORE arrival, since the waiting list is extremely long in September/October. My last gold nugget would be to not bother with opening a bank account (unless you get your ARC really early) and simply get a pre-paid Korean credit card. It is really easy and was simply a life saver!

Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
It was quite easy to find housing off campus. I know of many who found rooms through Airbnb, and I personally found my goshiwon through
goshipages.com
(which I highly recommend). I lived at 'Ace Residance'  (
https://goshipages.com/ace-residence
) which I was really happy with.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I would recommend finding housing through official sites like Airbnb or goshipages instead of facebook or instagram to avoid being scammed. Personally, I would also refrain from staying at share houses, since I've only heard people complain... But that might just be a few unfortunate cases.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Goshiwons are the way to go in my opinion ;)

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Be aware that the majority of courses are not available to exchange students! Most Underwood courses are unavailable (due to this I got none if the course I wanted pre-arrival, so I would NOT recommend planning your trip around any of the Underwood majors!) and just because a course is taught in English doesn't mean it will be available. In most cases, you can see which courses will be available in the course catalog BUT this is subject to change every year, so always have a plan B ready.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: There are three rounds of course registration. In the first round you are given a number of points to wage on the courses you want, BUT even if you place the maximum number of points on a course exchange students will always be prioritized last, so you are not guaranteed to get it. In the second round you can try your luck on other courses, if you didn't get the ones you liked in the first round, and in the third and final round you can drop courses or add ones that now have open spots.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The whole process was described in an email, but I would HIGHLY recommend to watch some youtube videos on the process!

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got none of the courses I initially wanted when choosing Yonsei (so don't apply for the Underwood majors!), but I ended up with 3 okay-ish courses.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Do some research into which courses are even available before applying to Yonsei, and once the process starts be prepared to settle for your plan B, C or even D.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Since I, unfortunately, had to settle for other courses than planned I ended up taking courses on subjects I didn't find all that interesting and were slightly below my level. It was okay, but I would definitely not say academics were the highlight of my exchange.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I had to do two 2nd year courses and a 3rd year course. I was technically considered a senior (4th year) at Yonsei, so the courses were definitely below my level.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: There was zero to no interaction with the students and we were not informed very well about the expectations and how we would be graded. It was actually quite frustrating that professors did not follow their own syllabi and the tests were not discussed at all in advance. It is also a complete mystery to me how we were graded, since in one of my courses I got a 64% on the midterm and a 32% on the final but ended up with a B+.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Design of polymeric materials
Organic chemistry 2 
Linear algebra and it's applications

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Design of polymers was by far the most interesting of my three courses, so I'd say it was worth it. The professor was quite good. 
I would not recommend organic chemistry 2 if you have already done anything similar at KU - it doesn't cover much new compared to the mandatory organic chemistry course on first year chemistry/nanoscience. At last, linear algebra was honestly quite boring BUT since it's such a useful topic, I would recommend it if you haven't already done a course on the subject.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There was quite a lot of clubs and activities geared towards international students hosted by the Global club.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The Global club arranged dance lessons, museum meet-ups, MTs, sports etc... It was quite competitive to be a part of some the clubs, but there were also a lot of one-time fun activities

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I heard a lot of good things about 'English society' which I sadly wasn't a part of... That i definitely regret! I'd also highly recommend to watch the Yonko games and take part in the Akaraka night.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Definitely visit Busan and/or Jeju if you get the chance. It was nice to get out of the huge city of Seoul and experience more of nature. I'd also recommend hiking in Bukhansan for the same reason. And if you like music be sure to go to at least one concert! It quite easy to get tickets through Interpark, Yes24 global, and Melon.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I didn't struggle to much with the cultural differences.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Take part in the mentor program! I got a very nice Korean mentor, Yuna, whom I became great friends with.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Being Caucasian I felt alienated at times. People don't assume you speak Korean, so people might talk about you, give you weird stares, and just generally make you feel different and out of place. That was one feeling I never really got used to.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: How many things there were to do in Seoul - alone and with friends. You'll never feel bored, and I really miss all the fun cafés, weird shops, and exciting foods

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Don't stress about academics! It's really difficult to plan your trip ahead, so you'll constantly have to make changes and you'll be more busy than you expect. So don't feel pressured to spend hours at the library. Take part in at least one club or mentor program - this was how I found the friends that carried me all the way through the semester. And lastly, the boring tips: find a SIM card online in advance (you'll save a lot of money!), do some research on the public transportation (buy a Tmoney card at the airport and take the subway from Incheon to Seoul - don't bother with the bus, it's a waste of money), begin the ARC process as soon as possible, and remember that you can get out of paying NHIS.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Things will not go as expected - get used to that thought ;)

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The thoughts and reflections about my life and my priorities. Getting away definitely gave me a new perspective on the things I've been dealing with back at home.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: More than once I felt overwhelmed and stressed. The loneliness got to me at times and I felt my exchange had to live up to unreasonably high expectations.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
